title: git checkout on Linux rewrites the working file in place — where the same operation on darwin replaced its identity

provenance.evidence: Two readings. `a.txt` KEEPS inode 550214 and goes 4 -> 12 bytes: the working file is rewritten in place, not replaced. `.git/HEAD` keeps its name and changes inode 550223 -> 550218, and `.git/index` likewise 550218 -> 550231 — both are rename-into-place. `.git/logs/HEAD` grows in place, 546 -> 693. Captured by tests/compatibility/save-patterns/v0/capture.mjs.
blind_spots: open, flush, fsync and close are invisible to polling
polling cannot order the four changes within a single reading

objects.role: a.txt, the working file — one identity, rewritten in place

folder.fidelity: a backend that does not declare ObserveDurableBoundary
folder.omission_note: No omission is declared admissible: each of the four changes belongs to a different object, so dropping a reading loses an object rather than merging two views of one.

expected.meaningful_durable_change: The working tree is at branch `other`: a.txt holds twelve bytes and the repository's own HEAD and index agree with it. One durable change for one branch switch — and it is only meaningful once BOTH the working file and the repository metadata have settled.
expected.forbidden_note: Mount 4 is the trap. The working file has closed and looks complete, so a Closed-anchored trigger would fire — but `.git/HEAD` has not yet been renamed into place, so the checkpoint would record a workspace whose file contents say `other` and whose repository says `master`. A checkpoint of a self-inconsistent repository is worse than a late one.

notes: SECOND CROSS-PLATFORM DIVERGENCE. The darwin capture (git-checkout-switch-branch) records a.txt VANISHING at one inode and reappearing at a new one. On Linux the same git operation, one minor version apart, keeps the inode and rewrites in place. Object identity across a checkout is therefore a platform property, not a git property.

The consequence for coalescing is asymmetric: on darwin the working file's identity change is a rename the coalescer must not span; on Linux there is no such rename and the same save looks like an ordinary in-place write. A rule that keys on identity change would treat the two platforms' identical user action as two different kinds of event.

Three candidates are offered and only the last is meaningful. This is the clearest case in the corpus for why a candidate is recorded rather than acted on: two of the three would checkpoint a repository mid-switch.
